definition: Probabilistic latent semantic analysis (PLSA), also known as probabilistic latent semantic indexing (PLSI, especially in information retrieval circles) is a statistical technique for the analysis of two-mode and co-occurrence data.
details: In effect, one can derive a low-dimensional representation of the observed variables in terms of their affinity to certain hidden variables, just as in latent semantic analysis, from which PLSA evolved. Compared to standard latent semantic analysis which stems from linear algebra and downsizes the occurrence tables (usually via a singular value decomposition), probabilistic latent semantic analysis is based on a mixture decomposition derived from a latent class model.

explainer.lead: Probabilistic latent semantic analysis is a statistical technique for analysing two-mode and co-occurrence data, yielding a low-dimensional representation via hidden variables. It matters as the probabilistic descendant of latent semantic analysis.

tiers.eli5: It looks at which things appear together and groups them by hidden themes, so similar items end up represented by the same underlying topics.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use PLSA (also called PLSI in information retrieval) to uncover latent topics in co-occurrence tables such as document-word counts. A pitfall is that it is a latent class mixture decomposition, not a linear-algebra downsizing, so the modelling assumptions differ from standard LSA.
tiers.paperLevel: PLSA derives a low-dimensional representation of observed variables in terms of affinity to hidden variables, like latent semantic analysis from which it evolved; unlike LSA's singular value decomposition of occurrence tables, it is based on a mixture decomposition derived from a latent class model.

explainer.example: A document-word occurrence table is decomposed so each document is described by its affinity to a small number of hidden topics.
